deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. There are no formulas, computations or derivations. It continues a natural-philosophical argument about teleology (Zweckmäßigkeit), drawing on G. T. Fechner, especially the 'Erdseele' (earth-soul) thesis of Zend-Avesta (1851) and Nanna (1848).

The logical structure, restated:

(0) Premises from the previous page:
- (P1) The only purposiveness whose cause we directly perceive is that of our own actions, and its cause is thinking. So for any observed purposiveness we can only seek its cause in a thought-process (Denkprozess).
- (P2) A closed system of changing, interlocking purpose-and-effect relations in a body is most probably explained by a unified thought-principle in that body, under two conditions. (i) The purposiveness does not split into sub-systems closed within parts of the body. (ii) There is no reason to seek its cause in a larger whole to which the body belongs.
- On the previous page, organic (bodily) purposiveness is assigned to a larger whole, for three reasons: it is not closed within the individual; it repeats innumerably; and it does not develop further within the individual's life.

(1) This page, first step. Subtract the organic purposiveness. What remains is a closed system of interlocking, variable purpose/effect relations:
- in humans and animals, admittedly (reading uncertain, see corrections);
- in plants, according to Fechner's view.
By (P2) this is explained by a unified thought-principle within them, i.e. an individual soul. Inner perception confirms this.

(2) Applying the same principles, the cause of organic purposiveness is sought in a unified thought-principle in the Earth.
- (a) Condition (i) holds. Organic purpose-relations on Earth do not split into separate systems; everything interlocks. So no plurality of partial principles in parts of the Earth suffices.
- (b) Condition (ii) holds: as far as experience reaches, there is no reason to go to a larger whole.
  - (b1) Organic purposiveness is closed on Earth. Organisms are made only for life on Earth, so the state of the Earth's crust contains all the reasons for their arrangement.
  - (b2) It is individual. It presumably does not repeat on other celestial bodies.
  - (b3) It does not stay constant over the Earth's life. Ever more perfect organisms appear. So the cause must be a thought-principle that simultaneously progresses to higher stages. This contrasts with point 3 of the previous page, where non-development ruled out a simultaneous process within the individual.

(3) Conclusion. From the standpoint of exact natural science, understood as explanation from causes, the assumption of an earth-soul (Erdseele) is a hypothesis explaining the existence and the history of organic nature.

The form is a two-criterion inference to the best causal explanation (closure plus no larger whole), applied in parallel at two levels: individual organism and Earth.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible, since there is no mathematics. As philosophy, step (b2), that organic purposiveness does not recur on other celestial bodies, is an empirical assumption that Riemann himself explicitly hedges ('Nach Allem, was wir wissen').

Step (b3) treats progressive appearance of more perfect organisms as requiring a simultaneously progressing thought-principle. This is a non-demonstrative inference that excludes non-teleological (e.g. Darwinian, 1859) explanations without argument.

results.what: Argument for an 'Erdseele' (earth-soul) as the hypothetical cause of the purposiveness and history of organic nature, via a closure criterion plus a no-larger-whole criterion for ascribing a unified thought-principle
results.modern_name: Teleological / panpsychist inference to the best explanation (Fechnerian earth-soul thesis)
results.usually_credited_to: G. T. Fechner (Nanna 1848, Zend-Avesta 1851); Riemann's engagement is known

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely natural-philosophical text with no mathematical content. Riemann's sympathy for Fechner's psychophysics and earth-soul ideas is well documented: related fragments 'Zur Psychologie und Metaphysik' were printed in Weber/Dedekind's edition of the Werke. This page fits that known material.
transcription_corrections: Line 2: 'unwidersprechlich[?]' should more likely read 'anerkanntermaßen'. The image shows a word ending in '-termaßen', and the sense is 'in humans and animals admittedly, in plants according to Fechner'.
'Denkprincipe' (lines 5-6 and later) appears correct, though in places it could be read 'Denkprocesse'. The image supports 'Denkprincipe' in the final occurrences ('fortschreitenden Denkprincipe').
The rest of the transcription is consistent with the image.
